source.title: Large Scale Language Modeling: Converging on 40GB of Text in Four Hours
source.authors: Raul Puri; R. Kirby; N. Yakovenko; Bryan Catanzaro

record.tranche_reason: The study varies batch size and reports held-out language-model and transfer results using an RNN language-model setup, testing the large-batch generalization claim with a different model family and task.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own batch-size results in Figures 5 and 6. Other claims about batch-size methods in cited work are background and are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: The study directly varies batch size and learning-rate schedules in an Amazon Reviews mLSTM language model. Figure 5 tests held-out performance after one epoch; Figure 6 tests whether schedule changes and longer training reduce the large-batch penalty.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that very large batches worsen evaluation quality without suitable schedule changes, and excessive learning-rate scaling can cause divergence. Longer training and a modified decay schedule bring large-batch BPC and transfer accuracy close to smaller-batch results, while a residual BPC difference remains.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains an mLSTM language model on Amazon Reviews with Adam and varies batch size and learning-rate schedule; it does not reproduce the image-classification or language-model comparisons named in the version.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, initial learning rate, decay schedule, and number of iterations or epochs affect evaluation quality. The authors report divergence with linear or square-root learning-rate scaling at large batches, and better convergence with a shared 3e-3 schedule decayed over 100k iterations.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger mLSTM hidden states improve language-model evaluation BPC in Figure 4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing recurrent language-model capacity can improve held-out prediction; this experiment does not establish improvement beyond a zero-training-error width threshold.

record.peer_reviewed: Symposium on Computer Architecture and High Performance Computing
record.problems: The study reports no uncertainty estimates for these results. Its large-batch comparison changes training duration and learning-rate schedule, and some runs do not complete the planned decay by the end of 3 epochs.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 reports additional one-epoch results for several initial learning rates and scaling rules. Those flattened entries were not extracted because the table layout does not clearly associate every value with a batch, rule, and metric.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label generalization.
Widening beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; all relevant batch experiments use Adam.
Image classifiers, learning-rate warmup, normalization or regularization changes, and complete removal of the penalty at a matched epoch budget.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized training examples versus random examples.

missing.what: Figure 6b also reports held-out sentiment-transfer accuracy across batches: SST 90.6, 90.6, 91.2, 90.3, 90.1%; IMDB 92.1, 92.7, 92.3, 92.3, 90.4%. These show that recovery differs by downstream task, with a residual IMDB decline at batch 32768.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V5. Figure 5's fixed-one-epoch comparisons are explicitly declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing. Unequal training durations in R1–R5 are experimental conditions, not themselves evidence that V5 needs qualification; V5 already includes recovery through longer training and recipe changes. No uncertainty estimates establish whether the smallest BPC differences are meaningful.

versions.untested_parts: Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD.
The study tests language models, not image classifiers; its batch sizes, schedules, and training durations do not cover all workload-dependent settings in the version.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the train-test gap.
